newsitem.title: UK: Pound rally promises soft landing for UK.
newsitem.headline: Pound rally promises soft landing for UK.

text.p: British manufacturers may be lining up to curse the strong pound which makes their products more expensive overseas, but the currency's rally will help ensure the economy does not overheat, economists said on Wednesday.

With economic growth widely expected to hit 3.25 to 3.5 percent in 1997 and the threat that interest rates will rise after a national election expected in May, analysts say sterling's rally will slow the economy and keep a keep a firm cap on inflation.

"Sterling's strength will take the edge off the economy as export growth weakens...1998 is likely to be a weaker year than 1997 and we are forecasting a fall in growth to 2.5 percent (next year)," said Roger Bootle, group chief economist at HSBC Markets.

Britain has enjoyed four years of strong growth and the output gap between potential and actual economic output has narrowed sharply. That makes a return to slower growth rates desirable to avoid a repeat of the late 1980s economic boom which ended in a bust because of spiralling consumer spending.

Sterling's trade-weighted index is now up 18 percent from a year ago, the swiftest rise since oil prices drove the pound higher in 1980-81 and some five percent higher in real terms than its average level since 1970.

With Britain's opposition Labour Party widely expected to form a new government within the two months, economists said the pound's rise will assist the early months of economic management for the centre-left party which has been out of power since 1979.

Labour's electoral performance has been hampered for decades by a legacy of suspect economic management in the 1970s, but the party may enjoy a relatively easy ride in terms of running the economy during the first two years of their administration.

As well as making sure growth returns to the trend rate of 2.5 percent seen over the past four decades, weak inflation pressures should only force the new Labour chancellor to raise interest rates by between 0.25 and 0.5 of a percentage point in 1997 from the current six percent, many economists forecast.

Even the ultra-hawkish Bank of England has toned down its advice on interest rates in recent months in the light of sterling's strength and other indicators. The central bank is now seeking just a quarter point rise in rates rather than the half point jump the central bank earlier pencilled in for early 1997.

Some economists even suggest the pound's rally and, in the event of a Labour victory, a pre-emptive tightening of fiscal policy in a mini-budget in late May or early June could allow base rates to stay at six percent, marking the longest period of low borrowing costs in Britain since the 1960s.

"There is an outside chance that either a further significant rise in sterling or a post-election fiscal tightening will allow base rates to stay at six percent this year," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.

Saunders has cut his forecast for growth in the economy this year to 3.0 percent from 3.3 percent, noting that sterling's real trade-weighted exchange rate is now similar to the average level when Britain was in Europe's exchange rate mechanism -- a period in which exports grew very slowly.
"UK export growth in 1997-8 will again probably slip to one to two percent below the OECD norm," Saunders said, enough to cut about 0.5 percent off the growth of gross domestic product (GDP).
So net exports are likely to be a slight drag on growth in 1997 and 1998, he said, whereas over the past four years net exports have added an average of 0.50 to 0.75 percent per year to GDP growth.

But like all golden economic scenarios there is a lingering danger the pound could rally too far, analysts warn. That could push manufacturing industry into a fresh downturn, denting industrial investment and making the economy even more reliant on continued consumer spending for growth.

British manufacturers are struggling with the strength of the pound. Data on Wednesday showed manufacturing output up just 0.3 percent and 1.6 percent year on year, but at least still expanding after a recent pause in growth.
